description:
Hi, I’m interested in computer science and space. I code in JavaScript, HTML, and CSS and enjoy building interactive projects like games and data-driven web apps. I’m looking for teammates who want to build something polished and finish on time.

Looking for: a designer or artist, someone strong in data or Python, and someone who can help with video and the writeup. Beginners are welcome, and all you need is some curiosity and a few free hours.
summary: Outpost Commander is a free browser game where kids ages 7 to 12 run a Moon or Mars outpost for 12 weeks. Players pack limited cargo, then balance power, air and water, food and radiation shielding while real solar flares from NASA's space weather database, dust storms and broken equipment test their plan. No choice is free: going to the storm shelter protects the crew but costs power and science time, and asking Mission Control for help works instantly on the Moon but too slowly on Mars. It matters because kids learn the real engineering trade-offs behind deep space survival, not just facts.
details:
What it does: Players choose the Moon or Mars, spend a cargo budget on solar panels, batteries, a nuclear reactor, greenhouses, a life support recycler, radiation shielding, food and air and water, and then run 12 weekly turns. Each week they pick a crew focus (science, farming, maintenance or rest) and react to events: solar storms, a dust storm, night on the Moon, and a failing recycler filter. A forecast shows what each choice would do before they commit, and each week ends with a plain-language "Real science" fact. If the mission fails, the game explains what went wrong so the player can try a different plan.

How it works: Each mission is a small simulation with four things to watch: power, air and water, food and radiation. The game loads real solar flares from NASA DONKI and replays the last 12 weeks as radiation events. A bigger flare gives a bigger event. If live data cannot be loaded, it clearly labels archived examples of real flares instead. Shielding blocks solar storm radiation well but deep-space radiation only a little, and every defense costs cargo, power or crew time.

Benefits: Kids practice systems thinking by seeing that every decision has a cost, which is how real mission planners work. The game runs in any browser with no download or account, uses plain language with in-context definitions, and plays differently each time.

What we hope to achieve: To make deep space trade-offs something a 7 to 12 year old can feel and talk about, and to give classrooms a free way to start that conversation.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks), NASA DONKI API, NASA RadLab API, NASA Image and Video Library API, GitHub Pages for hosting.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI: real solar flares set the radiation storms in each mission.
NASA RadLab (OSDR): a real space station dose measurement shown next to the game's radiation numbers.
NASA Image and Video Library : real photos of Mars rovers, the Moon, and the Sun.
Curiosity rover radiation measurements (Hassler et al., Science, 2014) set the Mars radiation baseline. Details of how each one is used are in DATASETS.md in the repository.
projectRefs: Chang'e-4 lander Moon radiation measurement (Zhang et al., Science Advances, 2020) for the Moon baseline.
Fonts: Inter and Space Grotesk (Google Fonts, SIL Open Font License).
